commitResults.messageTitle: Add greeting and exit
Add support for echo
Add support for storing and listing tasks
Add mark and unmark commands
Add Todo, Deadline and Event task types
Add error handling using custom exception
Add delete command and use ArrayList
Use enum for command types
Add automatic saving of tasks to disk
commitResults.messageBody:
The task list currently lives only in memory, so every task a user adds
is lost the moment the chatbot exits.

Serialise each task into a single pipe-separated line and rewrite the
whole file to ./data/nova.txt after every change to the list. Rewriting
the file rather than appending keeps it consistent with marking and
deletion, at negligible cost for a list of this size.

The path is built with Path.of and is relative to the project root, so
it behaves the same on every OS, and the enclosing folder is created on
demand. The generated folder is git-ignored since it holds user data.

commitResults.messageTitle: Load saved tasks on startup
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks are written to disk but never read back, so the save file is
effectively write-only and a restart still shows an empty list.

Read ./data/nova.txt at startup and rebuild each task from its line.
A missing file is treated as an empty list rather than an error,
because it is the normal state the first time someone runs the chatbot
on a new machine.

Validate every line and skip the ones that do not parse, reporting how
many were dropped. Losing a single hand-edited or truncated line is far
better than refusing to start or discarding the whole list.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-7 into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 7 adds persistence: the task list is saved to ./data/nova.txt
after every change and reloaded when the chatbot starts.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store deadline and event times as LocalDateTime
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadlines and events keep their times as free-form strings, so the
chatbot cannot tell that "2/12/2019 1800" is a moment in time. That
rules out anything that needs to compare or reformat dates.

Introduce a DateTimes helper that parses the common ways a user might
write a date (yyyy-MM-dd and d/M/yyyy, each with an optional HHmm or
HH:mm time) and hold the result in Deadline and Event as LocalDateTime.

Display uses the friendlier "MMM dd yyyy" form, with the time appended
only when one was supplied; a bare date is stored as midnight and that
is the signal to leave the time out. The save file keeps ISO-8601 text
so values round-trip exactly, and unparseable input is rejected with a
message showing an accepted format.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add on command to list tasks for a date
commitResults.messageBody:
Now that deadlines and events carry real date-time values, the natural
next question a user has is "what do I have on this day?", which the
chatbot still has no way to answer.

Add an "on <date>" command that lists every task falling on the given
date. Each task decides for itself whether it matches, via an isOn
method: a deadline matches its due date, an event matches any day in
its span, and a plain todo never matches. Putting the test on the task
keeps the command free of type checks and leaves room for future dated
task types.

This covers the stretch goal of the Level 8 increment.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-8 into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 8 teaches the chatbot about dates: deadlines and events store
LocalDateTime values, display them in a friendly format, and can be
looked up by date with the new 'on' command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui class for all console interaction
commitResults.messageBody:
Nova mixes three unrelated jobs: reading input, deciding what to do,
and printing output. Every message is a System.out.println buried in
the middle of the command handling, so changing the wording of one
reply means editing the control flow.

Move all reading and printing into a Ui class that owns the Scanner and
the divider line, and give it a named method per message. Nova now says
what it wants shown rather than how to show it, which shortens each
command branch and puts every user-facing string in one file.

This is the first step of the A-MoreOOP increment; Storage, TaskList
and Parser follow.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Storage class for save-file handling
commitResults.messageBody:
Nova still owns the save file: the path, the pipe-separated line format,
the folder creation and the per-field validation all sit alongside the
command handling, which is the largest single reason the class is hard
to read.

Move that work into a Storage class that takes the file path in its
constructor and exposes load and save. Storage no longer prints; it
throws NovaException when the file cannot be read or written, and
counts the lines it had to skip, leaving Nova to decide what the user
sees. That separation also makes the file format testable on its own.

Second step of the A-MoreOOP increment; TaskList and Parser follow.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract TaskList to own the task collection
commitResults.messageBody:
The task list is a bare ArrayList passed from method to method, so code
that belongs to the collection ends up in the caller. The date search
for the "on" command, for instance, is written as a loop inside the
command handling.

Wrap the collection in a TaskList class with add, remove, get, size and
getTasksOn, and hand out only an unmodifiable view for display and
saving. The "on" command is now a single call, and future list-wide
operations have an obvious home.

Third step of the A-MoreOOP increment; Parser follows.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Parser and a Command class per instruction
commitResults.messageBody:
Even after Ui, Storage and TaskList moved out, the main loop is one
long switch: each branch pulls apart the input, changes the list, saves
it and prints a reply. Adding a command means growing that switch, and
the string handling stays tangled with the control flow.

Split the two halves. Parser turns a line of input into a Command
object, so all the substring and delimiter work lives in one class.
Each Command subclass then carries out one instruction through the
common execute(TaskList, Ui, Storage) method, and reports whether the
chatbot should exit. Nova shrinks to wiring plus a loop that parses,
executes and asks isExit.

Rename the old Command enum to CommandType, since the name is now taken
by the abstract command class, and give it an argumentsIn method so the
keyword lengths are no longer hard-coded as substring offsets.

Task numbers are range-checked at execution rather than at parse time,
because the parser has no view of the list. Loading stays in run rather
than the constructor so that a warning about a damaged save file still
appears below the welcome message.

This completes the A-MoreOOP increment, including its stretch goal.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-MoreOOP into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Break the single Nova class into Ui, Storage, TaskList, Parser and a
Command class per instruction.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organize classes into nova packages
commitResults.messageBody:
Nineteen classes now sit loose in the default package, so nothing in the
file listing says which classes belong together, and every class is
visible to every other one.

Group them into three packages under src/main/java, which stays the
source root:

* nova - the app itself: Nova, Parser, Storage, TaskList, Ui,
  DateTimes and NovaException
* nova.task - Task and its subtypes
* nova.command - the Command hierarchy and the CommandType keywords

The task and command families were the two obvious clusters; the
remaining classes are single collaborators of the app, so splitting
them further would have produced packages of one class each.

nova and nova.command do refer to each other, since Parser produces
commands and commands act on Ui, Storage and TaskList. That is accepted
here rather than worked around, as the alternative is an extra
indirection layer for no practical gain at this size.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Packages into master
commitResults.messageBody: Group the classes into the nova, nova.task and nova.command packages.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge add-gradle-support into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Bring in the Gradle build files provided with the project template:
the wrapper, build.gradle, and the matching .gitignore entries.

commitResults.messageTitle: build.gradle: Point application at nova.Nova
commitResults.messageBody:
The Gradle files that ship with the project template name
seedu.duke.Duke as the main class, which does not exist in this
project, so gradlew run fails immediately after the merge.

Set mainClass to nova.Nova, the entry point after the A-Packages
increment. Verified with gradlew build and gradlew run.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for DateTimes and the task types
commitResults.messageBody:
The project has no automated tests, so every change has to be checked
by hand at the console, and quiet mistakes in formatting or date
handling can survive unnoticed.

Add JUnit 5 tests for the two classes with the most logic per line:
DateTimes, which parses and formats every date the user types, and the
Task hierarchy, whose toString, toFileString and isOn methods define
what the user sees and what ends up on disk. Test methods are named
featureUnderTest_testScenario_expectedBehavior.

Writing them turned up a real defect: DateTimeFormatter resolves
leniently by default, so "2019-02-30" was silently accepted as 28 Feb
rather than rejected. Switch the input formatters to strict resolution,
which also means using the uuuu year pattern in place of yyyy.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for Parser, TaskList and Storage
commitResults.messageBody:
The first batch of tests covers date handling and the task types, which
leaves the three classes that carry the rest of the logic untested:
Parser turns text into commands, TaskList answers questions about the
collection, and Storage owns the save-file format.

Cover them:

* ParserTest checks that each keyword produces the right Command
  subclass and that every rejection path reports the expected message,
  since those messages are the user's only feedback.
* TaskListTest covers ordering, removal, the date search across all
  three task types, and that the list is copied in rather than aliased
  and handed out read-only.
* StorageTest drives real files through a JUnit @TempDir, covering the
  round trip for every task type, folder creation, rewrite-on-shrink,
  blank lines, and eight distinct ways a line can be malformed.

CommandTypeTest also pins down keyword matching, including that
"todoread book" is not accepted as a todo.

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: State the test coverage target
commitResults.messageBody:
The project now has a JUnit suite, but nothing records what it is meant
to cover, so future work has no standard to hold to.

Document where tests live, how to run them, the naming convention, and
a coverage target of the top ~50% highest-value methods, together with
the expectation that tests are updated in the same commit as the code
they cover.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-JUnit into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a JUnit 5 suite covering DateTimes, the task types, Parser,
TaskList, Storage and CommandType, and make date parsing strict.

commitResults.messageTitle: build.gradle: Name the distributable JAR nova.jar
commitResults.messageBody:
The shadowJar task still produces duke.jar, the name inherited from the
project template, which does not match the chatbot the file contains.

Rename the output to nova.jar. Verified by copying build/libs/nova.jar
into an empty folder and running `java -jar "nova.jar"` there: the app
starts, accepts commands, and creates its own data folder alongside the
JAR, so the distributed file needs nothing else to run.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Jar into master
commitResults.messageBody: Package the app as a runnable fat JAR named nova.jar.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Javadoc to the remaining public classes and methods
commitResults.messageBody:
Most of the classes extracted during A-MoreOOP were documented as they
were written, but the older ones were not: the whole task hierarchy,
NovaException and Nova.main carry no header comments at all, and the
CommandType constants are bare.

Document every non-private class, constructor, field and method that
was still missing one, and say what the values mean rather than
restating the name, e.g. that a midnight time is how the code records
"the user gave a date but no time".

Also fix the one broken link (Parser is in another package, so the
reference needs its qualified name) and add explicit documented
constructors where the implicit one was being published undocumented.
Parser gets a private constructor, since it holds only static methods.

./gradlew javadoc now completes with no errors and no warnings.

commitResults.messageTitle: Tweak code to follow the Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The code was written before the coding standard applied to this project,
so a handful of details drift from it.

Bring them into line:

* Rename DateTimes.strict to createStrictFormatter, as methods are
  named with verbs.
* Rename the loop variable c to type in CommandType.fromInput, since
  single letters are reserved for loop counters.
* Narrow the fields of Task, Deadline and Event from protected to
  private, and make the ones that never change final. Nothing outside
  each class reads them, so the wider scope was not buying anything.
* Replace the bare 3, 4 and 5 in Storage's line validation with named
  constants that say which task type each count belongs to.

Checked at the same time and already compliant: 4-space indentation,
no tabs, lines within 110 characters, no wildcard imports, K&R braces
with no brace-less if bodies, and case labels indented inside switch.

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Record the Java and Git standards
commitResults.messageBody:
The project now follows the SE-EDU Java coding standard and Git commit
conventions, but nothing in the repository says so, so the rules have to
be remembered rather than looked up.

Write both down, listing the points that actually come up in this code
rather than restating the whole guide, and link to the source for the
rest. Also state plainly that commit messages and pull requests carry no
AI attribution or co-author trailers.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add find command to search task descriptions
commitResults.messageBody:
Once the list grows past a screenful, the only way to locate a task is
to read through everything "list" prints, and the task number needed by
mark, unmark and delete has to be counted by eye.

Add "find <keyword>", which lists the tasks whose description contains
the keyword. The match ignores case and matches inside words, so "book"
finds both "read book" and "Bookkeeping"; someone searching for a
half-remembered task benefits more from a few extra hits than from an
exact match.

The test lives on Task as hasKeyword rather than in the command, so it
only sees the description and not the formatted date. Searching for
"Dec" therefore does not turn up everything due in December, which
would be surprising from a description search.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-JavaDoc into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Document the remaining public classes, constructors, fields and
methods; ./gradlew javadoc now runs clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-CodingStandard into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Tweak the code to follow the SE-EDU Java coding standard, and write
both the Java and Git standards down in AGENTS.md.

Conflicts in Task, Deadline and Event: A-JavaDoc documented the fields
while A-CodingStandard narrowed them from protected to private final.
The two changes are complementary, so both were kept, i.e. documented
private final fields.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-9 into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a find command that lists the tasks whose description contains a
given keyword.

Conflict in CommandType: A-JavaDoc gave every constant a comment while
Level-9 appended a new FIND constant. Kept the comments and documented
FIND to match.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Checkstyle to enforce the coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The Java coding standard is written down in AGENTS.md, but nothing
checks it. Compliance depends on remembering the rules while writing
and on catching lapses by eye during review, which does not scale.

Add the Gradle checkstyle plugin with the configuration from se-edu's
addressbook-level3, which encodes the same standard the project already
follows, plus its suppressions file exempting test classes from the
type and method Javadoc requirements. Checkstyle runs as part of the
check task, so gradlew build now fails on a style violation.

The main sources passed on the first run. The one violation was in
ParserTest, where a wrapped argument list left an opening parenthesis
at the start of a continuation line; the arguments are regrouped so the
parenthesis stays with the call.

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Mention Checkstyle in the coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard section lists the rules but not the fact that they
are now checked automatically, so it reads as something to apply by
hand.

Say where the configuration lives, how to run Checkstyle on its own,
and that violations should be fixed rather than suppressed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-CheckStyle into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Enforce the Java coding standard with Checkstyle, using the se-edu
configuration, wired into the Gradle check task.

commitResults.messageTitle: Return replies as text instead of printing them
commitResults.messageBody:
Ui writes straight to System.out, so the chatbot's replies only exist
as console side effects. A second front end cannot reuse any of them,
and the wording is not reachable from a test.

Collect the messages in a buffer instead and hand them over with
flush(). The divider lines move out of Ui and into the console front
end, since they are a console convention rather than part of what the
chatbot says.

Nova gains getGreeting, loadTasks and getResponse, each returning the
text for one step, plus isExit. run() is now a thin console loop over
those, and a GUI can drive the same three methods.

Console output is unchanged, including the case where a damaged save
file puts a warning in its own block below the greeting.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a JavaFX GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot is usable only from a terminal, which is a poor fit for
something meant to be handed to someone as a finished app.

Add a JavaFX front end: a scrolling conversation of dialog boxes, a
text field and a Send button. Both the field and the button trigger the
same handler, so Enter works as well as clicking. The newest message is
kept in view by binding the scroll position to the container height,
and "bye" disables the input and closes the window after a moment, so
the goodbye is readable rather than vanishing instantly.

The GUI drives the same getGreeting, loadTasks and getResponse methods
as the console front end, so there is one chatbot behind two interfaces
and no logic is duplicated. The console front end stays: it is far
easier to test than the GUI, and the regression checks run through it.

Entry point is Launcher rather than Main, since JavaFX will not launch
an Application subclass straight from a fat JAR.

JavaFX is declared as the tutorial does, listing every platform's
binaries so a JAR built on one machine runs on the others, with the
aarch64 classifiers added because Apple silicon needs its own natives.
The avatars are drawn rather than downloaded, as the tutorial's own
images are not fetchable.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-10 into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a JavaFX GUI in front of the existing chatbot, keeping the console
front end for testing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use varargs where it removes repetition
commitResults.messageBody:
Two places take a fixed handful of values and were written as repeated
single-value calls.

Ui built each reply with one addLine call per line, so a three-line
message was three statements that had to be read together to see the
shape of the reply. addLines now takes the lines as varargs, and each
show method is a single call whose arguments are the message.

TaskList.add takes Task... instead of one Task. Existing callers are
unaffected, since a single argument still matches, and test setup that
built a list of four tasks in four statements is now one.

Both are cases where the count is known at the call site and the values
are the same kind of thing, which is what varargs is for; the parser
and storage code takes arrays it is handed rather than lists it writes
out, so nothing there changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Varargs into master
commitResults.messageBody: Use varargs for Ui's line building and TaskList.add.
